Flow Lenia / Morphology and behavior / May–September 2026

Mapping the shapes
of Flow Lenia

A region selected from the geometry of 25,167 simulated forms turned out to lie closer to fish landmark shapes. That resemblance raises a harder question: how much can a map of shape tell us about what a body will do?

Distance to fish5.90 → 3.30

Median nearest-fish distance in normalized shape coordinates: full sample → selected region. Fish data played no part in selecting its 256 specimens.

01 / An unexpected resemblance

A region found without fish data lies closer to fish

We first selected 256 Flow Lenia specimens around a loop in the synthetic shape map. Only then did we compare them with two external datasets: 3D landmarks measured on real fish and snapshots from EmbryoMaker, a simulation of tissue development.

For each Lenia specimen, we measured the distance to its nearest neighbor in each external dataset. Across the broad Lenia sample, the median distance is smaller to EmbryoMaker. In the selected region, that ordering reverses: fish are nearer and EmbryoMaker forms are much farther away.

How the fish views and distances are constructed

The four fish use the source study’s size-normalized landmark coordinates and a common display scale. They are rotated to align the snout-to-tail axis and dorsal direction; lengths on screen are not millimeters. The tissue image uses its own principal plane and display scale. For the twelve-coordinate comparison, each absolute difference uses the original analysis normalization. Euclidean distance is the square root of the sum of squared differences.

All 256 members are closer to fish than to EmbryoMaker under this metric. The reported permutation comparison puts a shift this large at about one in a thousand random selections. Fish landmark shapes played no part in selecting the region, yet the selected forms concentrate nearer to them.

The resemblance is specific to the representation. Elongation, symmetry, and connectedness can place a simulated streak near a fish landmark configuration without making their anatomy or movement equivalent. Elongation drives much of the difference in the example above. Whether that explanation holds across the selected region, and under other representations of shape, remains to be tested.

02 / Building the comparison

Twelve measurements put three datasets in one space

Flow Lenia redistributes matter on a grid under local rules. Different rules produce different patterns. We reduce each resulting form to twelve coordinates, then apply the same measurements to 859 EmbryoMaker snapshots and 232 fish landmark configurations. Nearby points have similar measured shapes.

The coordinates describe elongation, directional bias, compactness, symmetry, connected components, coverage, boundary complexity, and enclosed gaps. They describe a shape’s geometry; they do not record its velocity, internal flow, or full generating rule. Fish landmarks and simulated mass distributions also represent bodies differently, so a shared coordinate system does not remove every difference between the datasets.

The twelve coordinates

Principal elongation; principal anisotropy; radial compactness; axial polarity; principal reflection symmetry; radial evenness; raster component count; largest component fraction; largest component anisotropy; raster coverage; boundary complexity; enclosure score.

Definitions are implemented in the common-morphology extractor. A separate 8,192-specimen Lenia cohort supplies a single-rule-family control.

Where the samples leave gaps

To find loops, we connect nearby forms and gradually widen the distance that counts as nearby. Some gaps fill quickly; others remain surrounded by connected forms over a wider range of distances. Persistent homology measures how long each loop lasts. The strongest loops in these samples have the following persistence lengths:

Largest loop persistence in each sampled cohort
CohortCalculationPersistence
Broad Flow Lenia · 25,1674,096-landmark approximation2.78
Single-family Lenia · 8,192Exact dense0.80
Fish landmark shapes · 232Exact dense0.64
EmbryoMaker · 859Exact dense0.29

All three datasets contain persistent loops. Their lengths depend on the sampled forms, sample size, and computation; the table does not isolate a biological or synthetic cause for the differences. A gap is an unoccupied region in this sample and representation, not proof that a form is impossible.

03 / Returning to the same measured shape

Most candidate loops fail the stricter rule-return test

Lenia lets us inspect something the shape coordinates omit: the parameters that generated each form. The loop experiment follows a sequence of nearby target forms back to the starting neighborhood, adjusting the rule along the way. It then compares the final rule state with the initial one.

An out-and-back path supplies the control. If the closed route leaves more difference in rule state than retracing a path, the route may matter even when the measured form returns. We tested that excess with two closure measures at three scales.

From the broad screen to dense checks

Initial screen
109 / 4,802groups pass both measures at all three scales
Broad-corpus dense rerun
1 / 5selected candidates survive both controls
Selected-region dense rerun
0 / 5selected candidates survive both controls

The dense checks test selected candidates, not random samples of all 4,802 groups.

Only one of the five broad-corpus candidates passed both dense checks; none of the five candidates from the region near fish did. The stronger calculations remove most of the apparent rule differences.

This leaves a specific problem to solve: determine whether the remaining rule difference persists under tighter transport and closure calculations. A reproducible difference would show information lost by the shape coordinates. Whether that information predicts behavior requires another experiment.

Permutation results and dense checks

The joint screen is marginal under permutation (p ≈ 0.094). Tests using either measure alone give stronger tails (p ≈ 0.008 for state closure and ≈ 0.0002 for the closure ratio), but the dense checks remove most candidates. There is one broad-corpus case worth following; the selected region near fish has no surviving joint witness among the five checked.

04 / From shape to behavior

One body.
Four possible encounters.

To study behavior, we turn to a separate cohort from later campaigns: five bodies that stayed coherent and moved. Each starts from the same saved state in four branches. Leave the path clear, or place an obstacle ahead, left, or right.

  1. 626specimens replayed
  2. 184remained coherent
  3. 9also moved
  4. 5could be tested

The 3,600-step replays screened for a persistent individual, then movement of at least half a body diameter. Five specimens qualified for clean paired encounters. All fifteen obstacle branches made contact; the chart compares each body’s median response across the three placements with its unobstructed continuation, or sham.

The two highest-scoring individuals retained about 30% of sham progress and turned 12–13°. The other three retained 9–17% and turned more sharply. That suggests a testable connection between temporal coherence and resistance to perturbation, though five bodies from two related rule families cannot establish it.

Total matter was conserved in every branch, as Flow Lenia’s dynamics require. Organization could still change: one specimen lost substantial connected-body coherence and nearly reversed in one placement. Progress, turning, and the persistence of the same body therefore need separate measurements.

The experiment establishes measurable differences in response. The next step is to test whether distance on the morphology map predicts them.

The next comparison

Do nearby shapes
respond alike?

Predict how a body reacts from its shape. Then give the model its generating rule, too. Does the extra information explain what shape misses?

What would make this a convincing test?

Expand the coherent-mover cohort and expose each body to the same perturbations. Hold out entire rule lineages when comparing the predictions, so a model must generalize beyond familiar families. Mirror the starting bodies to separate handedness from obstacle placement, then remove the obstacle to measure whether the same individual recovers.

This is the proposed next experiment. The current five-body assay has measured responses; neither prediction model has been fitted.

Sources and analysis dates

The morphology and transport results come from the May 2026 analysis summarized in The Geometry of a Synthetic Morphospace. The coherent-organism obstacle assay was completed on 2 September 2026. This overview separates the two cohorts and retains the stricter transport checks.
